title: Κόραξ καὶ Ἑρμῆς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 166. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κόραξ ὑπὸ παγίδος κρατηθεὶς ηὔξατο τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι λιβανωτὸν ἐπιθύσειν.
sentences.tr: Korax hypo pagidos kratētheis ēuxato tōi Apollōni libanōton epithysein.
sentences.l: A raven, having been caught by a snare, vowed to Apollo that he would burn frankincense upon the altar.
sentences.n: ἐπιθύω is to lay an offering on the altar and burn it there; λιβανωτός, frankincense, is a bloodless offering — no beast to be killed, which suits a bird's promise; the resin itself came from Arabia and was not cheap. εὔχομαι takes the future infinitive for what is promised. The raven is Apollo's own bird, so Apollo is the god he naturally calls on.

sentences.t: Σωθεὶς δὲ τοῦ κινδύνου τῆς ὑποσχέσεως ἐπελάθετο.
sentences.tr: Sōtheis de tou kindynou tēs hyposcheseōs epelatheto.
sentences.l: But having been saved from the danger, he forgot the promise.
sentences.n: ἐπιλανθάνομαι, 'to forget', takes the genitive of the thing forgotten; τοῦ κινδύνου beside it is a genitive of separation with σωθείς, 'saved out of the danger'. The two genitives sit side by side and the sentence turns on them.

sentences.t: Πάλιν δὲ ὑφ’ ἑτέρας κρατηθεὶς παγίδος, ἀφεὶς τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα, τῷ Ἑρμῇ ὑπέσχετο θῦσαι.
sentences.tr: Palin de hyph’ heteras kratētheis pagidos, apheis ton Apollōna, tōi Hermēi hypescheto thysai.
sentences.l: And again, having been caught by another snare, having let Apollo go, he promised to Hermes to sacrifice.
sentences.i: And when he was caught again by a second snare, he dropped Apollo and promised a sacrifice to Hermes.
sentences.n: ἀφείς is 'having let go, having released', used here of dropping a god as one drops a man. Hermes is the god of windfalls and of thieves, and so the natural second address for a bird who has already broken one vow. ὑπό becomes ὑφ’ before the rough breathing of ἑτέρας.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔφη· « Ὦ κάκιστε, πῶς σοι πιστεύσω, ὃς τὸν πρότερόν σου δεσπότην ἠρνήσω καὶ ἠδίκησας ; »
sentences.tr: Ho de pros auton ephē· « Ō kakiste, pōs soi pisteusō, hos ton proteron sou despotēn ērnēsō kai ēdikēsas ; »
sentences.l: But he said to him: « O most wicked one, how am I to trust you, who denied your former master and wronged him? »
sentences.i: But Hermes said to him: « You utter villain, how am I to trust you, when you disowned your first master and did him wrong? »
sentences.n: πῶς σοι πιστεύσω is deliberative, 'how am I to trust you'; πιστεύω takes the dative of the person trusted. δεσπότης, 'master', of a god over the bird that belongs to him — the raven has not merely broken a vow but changed owners. ἠρνήσω is aorist middle, ἠδίκησας aorist active; the two are simply strung together, each verb keeping its own habit of voice. The space before the question mark is Chambry's French typography.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οἱ πρὸς τοὺς εὐεργέτας ἀγνώμονες γενόμενοι ἐν περιστάσει ἐμπεσόντες οὐχ ἕξουσι βοηθούς.
sentences.tr: Hoti hoi pros tous euergetas agnōmones genomenoi en peristasei empesontes ouch hexousi boēthous.
sentences.l: That those who have proved thankless toward their benefactors, when they have fallen into a hard pass, will have no helpers.
sentences.i: The story shows that those who have proved thankless toward their benefactors, when they fall into a hard pass, will have no one to help them.
sentences.n: The moral opens with a bare Ὅτι, 'that' — a subordinator with nothing above it to govern. The introducing verb is not written in the Greek: the literal line leaves the gap where the page leaves it, and the idiomatic line supplies 'the story shows'. ἀγνώμων is the man who will not recognize what has been done for him. περίστασις is the tight place a man's circumstances close him into.
